misconceptions.statement: The absolute value of -5 is -5, because the bars do nothing.
misconceptions.why: Students see the bars as decoration and focus on the written sign.
misconceptions.fix: Absolute value is the distance from zero, so it is never negative; |-5| = 5.
misconceptions.root_belief: symbols are decoration, not instructions

misconceptions.statement: The absolute value of a number means just dropping the sign, even in an expression like |3-8|.
misconceptions.why: Students learn 'remove the minus' as a shortcut and apply it before computing.
misconceptions.fix: First work out the value inside the bars, then take its distance from zero; |3-8| = |-5| = 5.
misconceptions.root_belief: a shortcut rule applies without checking meaning

misconceptions.statement: -9 is greater than -2 because 9 is greater than 2.
misconceptions.why: Students compare the digits using whole-number order and ignore the sign.
misconceptions.fix: On the number line, the number further left is smaller, so -9 is less than -2.
misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from whole numbers works everywhere
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student difficulties ordering negative integers

misconceptions.statement: Any negative number is greater than zero if its digits are big.
misconceptions.why: Students treat the number as a size and forget that the sign puts it below zero.
misconceptions.fix: Every negative number lies to the left of zero, so it is smaller than zero and smaller than every positive number.
misconceptions.root_belief: bigger or more means more effect

misconceptions.statement: The minus sign always means 'take away', so -4 cannot be a number by itself.
misconceptions.why: Early school only shows minus as the subtraction operation.
misconceptions.fix: A minus sign can also show a number's opposite side of zero, as in -4, which is 4 steps left of zero.

probe.question: Is -4 a number you can mark on the number line?
probe.wrong_answer: No, minus means take away, it needs something to take from.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning
misconceptions.source_hint: research on students' interpretation of the minus sign as operation versus sign

misconceptions.statement: Subtracting a negative number makes the answer smaller, so 5 - (-3) = 2.
misconceptions.why: Students think subtraction always decreases and the minus signs are ignored or just cancelled to one.
misconceptions.fix: Subtracting -3 is the same as adding 3, so 5 - (-3) = 8.
misconceptions.root_belief: an operation always has the same effect
misconceptions.source_hint: research on integer subtraction errors in middle school

misconceptions.statement: Two minus signs side by side stay minus, so 4 - (-6) = -2.
misconceptions.why: Students notice the sign twice but do not know that they combine to plus.
misconceptions.fix: The two minus signs together turn into a plus, so 4 - (-6) = 4 + 6 = 10.
misconceptions.root_belief: repeating a symbol repeats its effect

misconceptions.statement: Subtracting in either order gives the same answer, so 3 - 8 = 8 - 3.
misconceptions.why: Students carry over the commutative habit from addition.
misconceptions.fix: Subtraction depends on order; 3 - 8 = -5 but 8 - 3 = 5.
misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from whole numbers works everywhere
misconceptions.source_hint: research on 'subtract smaller from larger' errors

misconceptions.statement: When adding numbers with different signs, the answer takes the sign of the first number.
misconceptions.why: Students pick the sign by position instead of by which number is bigger in size.
misconceptions.fix: The answer takes the sign of the number with the larger absolute value, and you subtract the sizes.
misconceptions.root_belief: position in a sentence decides importance

misconceptions.statement: Adding a negative number makes the total bigger because it is still an addition.
misconceptions.why: Students attend to the word 'add' and ignore the negative sign.
misconceptions.fix: Adding a negative number moves left on the number line, so the result is smaller.
misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning
misconceptions.source_hint: research on integer addition with negative addends

misconceptions.statement: Minus times minus is minus, because two negatives make something even more negative.
misconceptions.why: Students think more negatives pile up the negativity.
misconceptions.fix: A negative times a negative is positive; for example (-3) × (-4) = 12, as seen from the pattern of products.
misconceptions.root_belief: bigger or more means more effect
misconceptions.source_hint: research on students' reasoning about multiplying negative integers

misconceptions.statement: The rule 'two negatives make a positive' works for addition too, so -3 + (-4) = 7.
misconceptions.why: Students remember the slogan without knowing which operations it applies to.
misconceptions.fix: The slogan applies to multiplying or dividing; adding two negatives gives a bigger negative, so -3 + (-4) = -7.
misconceptions.root_belief: a rule works for every operation
misconceptions.source_hint: research on overgeneralising sign rules across operations

misconceptions.statement: A positive times a negative is positive because multiplication makes numbers bigger.
misconceptions.why: Students trust the whole-number idea that multiplying increases.
misconceptions.fix: Positive times negative is negative; 4 × (-3) is -3 added four times, which is -12.
misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from whole numbers works everywhere

misconceptions.statement: The product of several negative numbers is always positive.
misconceptions.why: Students extend 'minus times minus is plus' without counting the factors.
misconceptions.fix: The product is positive if the count of negative factors is even and negative if it is odd.
misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from two cases works for any number

misconceptions.statement: A negative number divided by a negative number gives a negative answer.
misconceptions.why: Students treat division as separate from multiplication rules and keep 'negative' as the answer's sign.
misconceptions.fix: Dividing two numbers with the same sign gives a positive answer, so (-12) ÷ (-3) = 4.
misconceptions.root_belief: more negatives means more negative result

misconceptions.statement: Removing brackets after a minus sign leaves the signs inside unchanged, so 10 - (3 - 5) = 10 - 3 - 5.
misconceptions.why: Students treat the bracket as just a grouping and forget the minus acts on everything inside.
misconceptions.fix: A minus before a bracket flips every sign inside, so 10 - (3 - 5) = 10 - 3 + 5 = 12.
misconceptions.root_belief: an operation affects only the nearest item
misconceptions.source_hint: research on errors in algebraic sign handling with brackets

misconceptions.statement: -3² means (-3) × (-3), so it equals 9.
misconceptions.why: Students read the minus as part of the number being squared.
misconceptions.fix: Without brackets only 3 is squared, so -3² = -(3×3) = -9, while (-3)² = 9.
misconceptions.root_belief: symbols are read left to right as one chunk
misconceptions.source_hint: research on calculator and textbook notation errors with negative bases

misconceptions.statement: The square of a negative number is negative, so (-4)² = -16.
misconceptions.why: Students keep the minus sign and do not notice two negatives multiply.
misconceptions.fix: (-4)² = (-4) × (-4) = 16, so the square of any non-zero number is positive.
misconceptions.root_belief: the sign stays the same after an operation

misconceptions.statement: A bracket next to a number means add, so 5(-3) = 2.
misconceptions.why: Students see two terms placed together and join them by addition or subtraction.
misconceptions.fix: A number next to a bracket means multiply, so 5(-3) = 5 × (-3) = -15.
misconceptions.root_belief: unwritten operation means the easiest operation

misconceptions.statement: When multiplying a bracket by a negative number, only the first term inside gets multiplied, so -2(3 + 4) = -6 + 4.
misconceptions.why: Students stop after the nearest term, as in the 'nearest item' habit.
misconceptions.fix: The multiplier applies to every term inside, so -2(3 + 4) = -6 - 8 = -14.
misconceptions.root_belief: an operation affects only the nearest item
misconceptions.source_hint: research on partial distribution errors in algebra

misconceptions.statement: In -2(3 - 5), the answer is -6 - 10 because the minus inside stays minus.
misconceptions.why: Students multiply the sizes and keep each original sign, ignoring the negative multiplier.
misconceptions.fix: Multiply each term by -2 including its sign: -2×3 = -6 and -2×(-5) = +10, so the answer is 4.
misconceptions.root_belief: the sign stays the same after an operation
misconceptions.source_hint: research on sign errors when distributing a negative factor
